BUILT AROUND YOUR ENVIRONMENT

Work with what
you already have.

We work with your existing teams, technology choices and approval processes. The starting point is the business requirement—not a predetermined model or a new platform to sell.

Scope, dependencies, decision rights and acceptance criteria are made explicit. That keeps the conversation grounded in what can be delivered and what will make it useful.

Our approach
A FEW PRACTICAL QUESTIONS

Before we begin.

Do we need a defined use case?

No. Discovery can start with a business priority or a recurring point of friction. The first step is to understand the workflow, the people involved and what a better result would look like.

Can you work with our delivery team?

Yes. We can work alongside your product, engineering, data and business teams with a clearly agreed remit and delivery responsibilities.

Do we need to replace our existing platforms?

Not by default. We assess how the requirement can fit your approved environment and identify where a new component is genuinely needed.

How are engagements scoped?

We agree the workstream, roles, expected outputs, dependencies and review cadence before starting. Hours or days and commercial terms are agreed for time-and-materials engagements.

Home/Services

The right problem.
A practical path forward.

Turn an AI mandate, a promising idea or an operational frustration into a requirement your business and delivery teams can act on.

Discuss this service
WHEN THIS HELPS

Recognise the
starting point?

01

Competing ideas, no shared priority

Bring business objectives, user needs and delivery realities into one discussion.

02

A sponsor needs a clearer case

Make assumptions, expected benefits, constraints and decisions visible before work expands.

03

Step back from the proposed technology and define what the workflow actually needs.

THE WORK

What we help
you put in place.

01

Discover the work

Map the current process, the people doing it, the information used and the friction worth addressing.

02

Frame the opportunity

Define the desired change, intended users, boundaries and a testable value hypothesis.

03

Assess practical fit

Review information access, system dependencies, quality expectations, ownership and the delivery environment.

04

Shape the next decision

Build a prioritised set of options, a clear requirement and a practical first increment.

WHAT YOU TAKE FORWARD

Useful work.
Clear outputs.

01

Discovery brief

A shared understanding of the problem, users, process and desired change.

02

Prioritised opportunities

An explicit view of candidate initiatives, assumptions and trade-offs.

03

Implementation outline

A first scope with key dependencies, responsibilities and acceptance criteria.

04

Decision-ready case

A concise recommendation with costs and benefits framed as assumptions to validate.

A USEFUL TEST OF PROGRESS

Progress means stakeholders can explain the problem, agree what is in scope and identify the evidence needed for the next decision.

A FEW PRACTICAL QUESTIONS

Before we begin.

Is this a long strategy exercise?

It does not need to be. We scope discovery around the decision you need to make and the depth of evidence it requires.

Will discovery always recommend AI?

No. A simpler process change, better access to information or conventional automation may be more appropriate for parts of the work.

Who needs to be involved?

Typically the business owner, people doing the work, and representatives who understand the data, systems and relevant controls. The exact group depends on the requirement.

A FEW PRACTICAL QUESTIONS

Will you choose a new model or cloud for us?

Can you integrate with legacy systems?

Does connecting a source mean every user can access it?

/services/workflows.title: Agentic workflows
/services/workflows.description: Design AI-enabled workflows that coordinate multiple steps, tools and people—with clear boundaries for what happens next.
/services/workflows.body:
Home/Services

Beyond a response.
Through the whole task.

Design AI-enabled workflows that coordinate multiple steps, tools and people—with clear boundaries for what happens next.

Discuss this service
WHEN THIS HELPS

Recognise the
starting point?

01

The work involves repeated handoffs

Define the sequence, required inputs and accountable owner for each step.

02

A single assistant cannot finish the task

Separate the capabilities, tools and checks needed to complete the business process.

03

Failures disappear between components

Make exceptions, recovery paths and human decisions part of the workflow design.

THE WORK

What we help
you put in place.

01

Define the task boundary

Specify the trigger, expected outcome, inputs, permissions and actions that are allowed.

02

Design the sequence

Connect reusable capabilities and tools with explicit handoffs and criteria for progressing.

03

Place human decisions deliberately

Identify which actions need review, approval or escalation rather than assuming full autonomy.

04

Design for exceptions

Specify what happens when a source is unavailable, a tool fails or an output does not meet the required standard.

05

Evaluate end to end

Test complete tasks using representative and adverse scenarios before widening the scope.

WHAT YOU TAKE FORWARD

Useful work.
Clear outputs.

01

Workflow definition

A process map with triggers, inputs, steps and completion conditions.

02

Control design

Permissions, approval points, exception handling and escalation routes.

03

Implementation increment

A scoped workflow or capability integrated with the agreed environment.

04

Evaluation pack

Task-level tests, observed failures and acceptance evidence.

A USEFUL TEST OF PROGRESS

Progress means the task can be completed predictably within its defined scope, and a person can understand where it stopped, why it stopped and who needs to act.

A FEW PRACTICAL QUESTIONS

Before we begin.

Does every workflow need several agents?

No. We choose the simplest structure that meets the requirement. A deterministic workflow, a single AI step or a combination of approaches may be more appropriate.

Can important actions remain under human control?

Yes. Approval and review steps can be designed into the workflow. The degree of autonomy is a business and governance decision, not a default.

What happens when something fails?

Failure handling is part of the design. Depending on the task, the appropriate response may be a retry, a safe stop, an alternative path or escalation to a named owner.

/services/adoption.body:
Home/Services

Built is a milestone.
Useful is the point.

Help people use AI in the work that matters, evaluate how it performs and build a grounded view of what should improve.

Discuss this service
WHEN THIS HELPS

Recognise the
starting point?

01

The capability exists, but use is uneven

Understand where it fits into people’s work and what makes it difficult to use.

02

Activity is visible, but impact is unclear

Connect usage signals with task quality, workflow change and the original business objective.

03

Every release creates more manual checking

Develop reusable evaluations, clearer acceptance criteria and a manageable feedback loop.

THE WORK

What we help
you put in place.

01

Understand the user’s task

Observe how people find, use and review the capability within their actual workflow.

02

Support adoption

Create task-based guidance, onboarding and feedback channels appropriate to the intended users.

03

Evaluate quality and reliability

Define representative tests, human review criteria and repeatable checks for important changes.

04

Build useful measures

Separate access, usage, quality, operational change and financial assumptions instead of treating them as interchangeable.

05

Improve from evidence

Bring findings into a regular review that informs product changes, enablement and the next scope decision.

WHAT YOU TAKE FORWARD

Useful work.
Clear outputs.

01

Adoption plan

A task-based approach to onboarding, guidance and feedback.

02

Evaluation framework

Representative scenarios, acceptance criteria and review responsibilities.

03

Evidence view

A structured picture of use, quality, workflow impact and remaining uncertainty.

04

Improvement backlog

Prioritised changes linked to observed friction and business needs.

A USEFUL TEST OF PROGRESS

Progress means intended users can complete relevant work, the quality is understood and product decisions are based on more than activity counts.

A FEW PRACTICAL QUESTIONS

Before we begin.

Can you guarantee adoption or a return on investment?

No. Those outcomes depend on the problem, implementation, users and operating environment. We help define the assumptions, address friction and evaluate the evidence.

Do you only measure usage?

No. Usage is one signal. We also consider task quality, completion, rework, user experience and the business outcome the initiative was intended to support.

Does this work with an existing rollout?

Yes. An existing capability and its current users can be the starting point. We first establish what is happening before recommending changes.

Close to your team.

We work alongside the people responsible for the outcome. The aim is not another layer of handoffs. It is a shared understanding of what needs to happen next.

Start a conversation

Business context first.

People in the picture.

HOW THE WORK MOVES

A practical rhythm.
Not a rigid playbook.

01

Understand

Agree the business problem, intended users, current workflow and what a useful result would look like.

02

Define

Make scope, dependencies, roles, controls and acceptance criteria explicit.

03

Connect

04

Evaluate

Review task quality, user experience, exceptions and the original value assumptions.

05

WHAT YOU TAKE FORWARD

Useful work.
Clear outputs.

01

A defined remit

A focused workstream or embedded contribution, with responsibilities agreed upfront.

02

A shared cadence

Regular reviews of progress, decisions, dependencies and outstanding issues.

03

Clear commercials

Time and materials based on agreed hours or days, with rates and scope confirmed before work starts.

04

A considered handover

A FEW PRACTICAL QUESTIONS

Before we begin.

Can we start with a small piece of work?

Yes. A focused discovery, integration assessment or defined delivery workstream can be a sensible starting point.

Will Dockio replace our team?

That is not the default model. We work alongside existing teams and agree where Dockio contributes, where your team owns delivery and how decisions are made.

What does founder-led mean?

Founder involvement is agreed as part of the engagement, including the remit and review cadence. It does not mean an undefined promise of unlimited availability.

What do you need before starting?

A business contact, a description of the work, relevant context and access to the people who understand the requirement. System and data access follow the approvals agreed for the engagement.

/insights/beyond-the-pilot.title: The pilot works. What happens on Monday?
/insights/beyond-the-pilot.description: A promising demonstration is the start of a delivery conversation—not the end of one.
/insights/beyond-the-pilot.body:
Home/Perspectives
IMPLEMENTATION · A DOCKIO PERSPECTIVE

The pilot works. What happens on Monday?

A promising demonstration is the start of a delivery conversation—not the end of one.

A different question

A pilot can show that an AI capability is possible. The next question is whether it can become part of a real person’s work. We approach that transition by looking beyond the model response and examining the whole task.

Follow the task, not just the output

Consider an illustrative internal knowledge assistant. A convincing answer is useful, but the employee also needs to know whether the source is appropriate, whether they are allowed to access it and what to do when the answer is incomplete. The delivery question includes all of those steps.

Make dependencies visible

Before expanding a pilot, we would map its approved sources, access requirements, interfaces, review steps and support responsibilities. A missing permission or an unsupported integration is not a minor detail when it prevents the intended task from being completed.

Test more than the happy path

A useful evaluation includes the cases people hope will not occur: unavailable sources, incomplete inputs, conflicting information and tool failures. For each one, define what the system should do and what the user should see. Sometimes the correct response is a clear stop rather than a confident continuation.

Name the operational owner

Someone needs to own source updates, issue triage, quality reviews and decisions about changes. These responsibilities should be discussed before a wider rollout. A handover document is useful only when the responsibilities in it are understood and accepted.

Choose the next increment

The next step does not have to be a broad release. It might be one connected task for a defined group, with an agreed review period and acceptance criteria. The aim is to learn whether the capability works inside the environment—not simply whether more people can open it.

A practical closing question

Instead of asking only, “Does the demo work?”, ask: “Can the intended user complete this task on an ordinary working day, and does someone know what to do when it does not work?” That is a more useful foundation for the next delivery decision.

Examples are illustrative. The right design depends on the requirement and the operating environment.

/insights/start-with-the-work.title: Start with a business problem, not an agent.
/insights/start-with-the-work.description: Choose the technology after the task is understood, not before.
/insights/start-with-the-work.body:
Home/Perspectives
STRATEGY · A DOCKIO PERSPECTIVE

Start with a business problem, not an agent.

Choose the technology after the task is understood, not before.

Let the problem set the direction

An AI conversation can quickly become a discussion about agents, models and orchestration. Our starting point is different: what is the business trying to change, who is doing the work and what is making that work difficult?

Describe the current workflow

Take an illustrative document-review process. The friction might be slow extraction, repeated information requests, inconsistent interpretation or unclear approval ownership. Those are different problems. Treating them as one request to “build an agent” hides the choices that need to be made.

Define the intended change

A useful requirement explains the users, the task, the inputs, the expected result and the boundary of the work. It also states what should remain under human judgement. This gives business and delivery teams something concrete to review.

Separate assumptions from evidence

Expected time savings, source quality and integration feasibility may initially be assumptions. Write them down as assumptions. Then identify what would validate them and which decision depends on the result. The point is not to eliminate uncertainty before starting; it is to stop uncertainty becoming an invisible commitment.

Choose the simplest suitable structure

Some parts of a process may need conventional automation. Others may benefit from AI-supported extraction or synthesis. Some should remain human decisions. We prefer a design that serves the requirement rather than one that maximises the number of agents or tools.

Make the first increment decision-ready

A first scope should be small enough to understand and meaningful enough to evaluate. Define the task it will complete, the dependencies it needs and the criteria for deciding what comes next.

The question to keep returning to

“What useful change will this make to the work?” is a better organising question than “How much AI can we put into this process?” It keeps the technology connected to the reason the initiative exists.

Examples are illustrative. The right design depends on the requirement and the operating environment.

Home/Perspectives
ADOPTION & VALUE · A DOCKIO PERSPECTIVE

Usage is a signal. It isn’t the whole story.

A useful review connects activity to the task and the change the initiative was meant to support.

Begin with the original objective

Usage can tell you that people are interacting with a capability. It does not, by itself, tell you whether they completed the intended task, trusted the output or improved the result. Our approach is to connect the review back to the original business objective.

Keep different measures distinct

Access, use, task quality and business impact answer different questions. Was the capability available to the intended people? Did they use it for relevant work? Was the result good enough? Did anything meaningful change in the workflow? Combining these into one success label makes the review less useful.

Look at completion and rework

Consider an illustrative drafting workflow. A draft may be produced quickly but require extensive correction. Another may take longer to generate yet be easier to review. A grounded evaluation looks at the task through completion, including the work performed by the reviewer.

Understand the reasons behind the pattern

Low usage is a prompt for investigation, not an automatic verdict. The task may be infrequent, access may be inconvenient or the capability may not fit the workflow. Speaking with intended users helps identify which of those explanations deserves attention.

Be careful when translating time into money

An estimate of time saved is not the same as a realised financial benefit. The business needs to explain what happens to that capacity and how any financial effect will be established. We prefer to make the assumptions visible rather than convert every activity signal into a return-on-investment claim.

Use the review to change something

A useful evidence review should lead to a decision: improve the workflow, change the guidance, address a quality issue, narrow the scope or extend a capability that is working. Measurement is valuable when it helps someone act.

Keep the picture connected

Usage belongs in the conversation. So do quality, reliability, user experience and the business outcome. The aim is not the largest activity number. It is a clearer understanding of whether the capability is becoming useful.

Examples are illustrative. The right design depends on the requirement and the operating environment.

/privacy.title: Privacy information
/privacy.description: How Dockio handles website visits, Microsoft Bookings and information you choose to share.
/privacy.body:
Home/Privacy

A little clarity
about your information.

How information moves when you visit Dockio or book a conversation.

Booking a meeting

Booking links open Dockio’s existing Microsoft Bookings page in a new tab. You choose an available time and enter your details on Microsoft’s service. This website does not collect or store the details you enter in Microsoft Bookings.

The booking page requests your name, email address and phone number, and asks questions about your role and technology context. Review the information on that page before confirming. Microsoft and Dockio handle the information needed to arrange the meeting through that service.

Information you choose to send

If you email Dockio, the message and the information you include are handled through the relevant email services. We use the information you provide to understand and respond to your enquiry and discuss the work with you.

Please do not include confidential client material, sensitive personal information or system credentials in an initial enquiry or booking.

Website storage and analytics

This website does not include advertising trackers, analytics scripts, or a contact form database. It does not save visitor entries in browser storage. The hosting, booking and email services may process technical information under their own policies.

Questions about your information

For questions about information you have sent to Dockio, or to request that we update or remove it, contact sankalp@dockio.in.
